newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OTK TRADES LOWER THAN EXPECTED ON DEBUT.
newsitem.headline: OTK TRADES LOWER THAN EXPECTED ON DEBUT.

text.p: Shares in South African grain processing and storage firm OTK Holdings Ltd started trading lower than expected on the former co-operative's first day as a listed company.
OTK shares opened at 520 cents each, before slipping back as low as 480 cents. At 1305 GMT the firm's stock was trading at 495 cents.

Analysts and dealers said the market had expected the group to open above 550 cents and possibly as high as 650 cents. They said that the bearish judgement was due to a falling stock market and the perception that the stock was exposed to risks.
"This is a fairly tough market to come into," one analyst said.
The stock market, concerned over the falling rand and delays in abolishing foreign exchange controls, fell for five straight sessions last week and opened down again on Monday.

Analysts said the deregulation of South Africa's maize market meant that the firm would become more exposed to the unpredictable whims of market forces in the volatile international commodities markets.
"The deregulation of the market will take away the certainty that went with the old system," said Gary Cloete, analyst at SMK Securities.

Last month South Africa's Maize Board said it will be dissolved and withdraw from the export market by the start of the 1997/98 season (May-April) if the industry is able to agree on a blueprint for a future marketing system by then.
Analysts also said the stock shared the characteristic of most agriculture-based firms in being exposed to the risks of natural distasters such as drought.
Despite the low trading price the shares were above their first pre-listing price.
The pre-listing offer to institutions, which was only 26 percent subscribed, was priced at 310 cents each. The remaining 74 percent of share capital is held by individuals.
In its listing statement the firm predicted it would post a net profit for the year to February 28 of 186.4 million rand on sales of 2.25 billion rand.
Analysts said the firm was based on a solid balance sheet and little debt.
Some speculated that the firm's shares should eventually move up and, in more favourable market conditions, could be fairly valued at between 600-640 cents each.

OTK, based in the northern South African province of Mpumalanga, last year transformed itself into a private company after operating as an agricultural co-operative since its establishment by a group of farmers in 1923.
